varieties.name: Henderson Bush
varieties.notes: Small-seeded baby lima on compact bushes; the earliest, surest lima where summers are short.

varieties.name: Jackson Wonder
varieties.notes: Speckled buff-and-purple butter bean; keeps setting pods through heat and dry spells in the South.

varieties.name: Fordhook 242
varieties.notes: Classic large-seeded bush lima that sets pods in hot weather; the standard for big, plump beans.

varieties.name: King of the Garden
varieties.notes: Vigorous pole lima with big flat beans and heavy yields; best where summers are long and warm.

varieties.name: Christmas
varieties.notes: Large maroon-splashed pole lima with chestnut flavor; thrives in long, hot summers.

varieties.name: Queen Anne
varieties.notes: Compact bush blackeye with an early, concentrated set; good for small gardens or shorter summers.

varieties.name: Mississippi Silver
varieties.notes: Silvery pods that are easy to shell; bred for heat, humidity and disease in Deep South gardens.

varieties.name: Pinkeye Purple Hull
varieties.notes: Southern favorite with purple pods that are easy to spot; often gives a second flush in hot climates.

varieties.name: California Blackeye No. 5
varieties.notes: The classic black-eyed pea; wilt- and nematode-resistant, productive for fresh shelling or dry beans.

varieties.name: Zipper Cream
varieties.notes: Large creamy-white peas from pods that 'zip' open; mild flavor, prized for fresh shelling in the South.

varieties.name: Early Sunglow
varieties.notes: Short plants with 7" yellow ears; very early and tolerates cool soil where summers are short.

varieties.name: Northern Xtra-Sweet
varieties.notes: One of the earliest supersweets; sugars hold well after picking. Isolate from other corn types.

varieties.name: Ambrosia
varieties.notes: Tender bicolor with 8" ears; a reliable mid-season sugary-enhanced choice for most gardens.

varieties.name: Bodacious
varieties.notes: Big 8" yellow ears with sweet, tender kernels; vigorous and dependable across most regions.

varieties.name: Golden Bantam
varieties.notes: 1902 heirloom with old-fashioned corny flavor; save your own seed. Eat right after picking.

varieties.name: Incredible
varieties.notes: Large 9" yellow ears with excellent flavor; a top main-season se for home and market growers.

varieties.name: Illini Xtra Sweet
varieties.notes: The original supersweet; very sweet and long-holding. Needs warm soil and isolation from other corn.

varieties.name: Silver Queen
varieties.notes: Late white corn with long ears and classic flavor; a Southern favorite where the season is long.

varieties.name: Minnesota Midget
varieties.notes: 4" melons on 3-ft vines; the go-to for short, cool summers, small spaces and containers.

varieties.name: Halona
varieties.notes: Early, very sweet orange melon with powdery mildew resistance; ripens well where summers are short.

varieties.name: Athena
varieties.notes: Eastern-type cantaloupe with firm sweet flesh and good shelf life; tolerant of fusarium and mildew.

varieties.name: Sugar Cube
varieties.notes: Softball-size, very high-sugar melons with broad disease resistance; ideal for small households.

varieties.name: Hale's Best Jumbo
varieties.notes: Old standard with thick salmon flesh; handles heat and drought well. Good where summers are long.

varieties.name: Ambrosia
varieties.notes: Exceptionally sweet, juicy flesh and small seed cavity; a flavor favorite where summers are long.

varieties.name: Mini Love
varieties.notes: AAS winner with short vines and 7-lb red melons; good for small gardens and cooler, shorter summers.

varieties.name: Blacktail Mountain
varieties.notes: Bred for cool nights; ripens 6–12 lb melons where summers are short, and handles heat too.

varieties.name: Sugar Baby
varieties.notes: Classic dark-green 8–10 lb icebox melon; dependable in short seasons and small spaces.

varieties.name: Crimson Sweet
varieties.notes: Striped 20–25 lb melons, very sweet; resists fusarium wilt and anthracnose. A reliable all-rounder.

varieties.name: Charleston Gray
varieties.notes: Long gray-green melons with tough rinds; disease resistant and well suited to hot Southern summers.

varieties.name: Jubilee
varieties.notes: Huge oblong striped melons (25–40 lb) for long, hot seasons; resistant to fusarium wilt.

varieties.name: Annie Oakley II
varieties.notes: Compact, early spineless hybrid; one of the best okras for northern gardens and short summers.

varieties.name: Jambalaya
varieties.notes: Compact plants with early, heavy yields of dark green pods; good for containers and shorter seasons.

varieties.name: Cajun Delight
varieties.notes: AAS winner that bears early and keeps producing; a good choice for cooler regions as well as the South.

varieties.name: Clemson Spineless
varieties.notes: The standard spineless okra since 1939; tall, productive and thrives in the hottest summers.

varieties.name: Burgundy
varieties.notes: AAS winner with red stems and pods that stay tender longer; ornamental and productive in heat.

varieties.name: Georgia Jet
varieties.notes: Fast-sizing, moist orange roots; one of the best choices where summers are short or cool.

varieties.name: O'Henry
varieties.notes: White-skinned, cream-fleshed Beauregard sport with a semi-bush habit; drier and less sweet.

varieties.name: Beauregard
varieties.notes: The most widely grown sweet potato; high yields, early and adaptable, stores well. Good for the North.

varieties.name: Covington
varieties.notes: Uniform, smooth roots with rich orange flesh; resists fusarium and root-knot nematode. Stores well.

varieties.name: Vardaman
varieties.notes: Bush-type with short vines and purple-tinged foliage; good for small gardens with a long season.

varieties.name: Murasaki
varieties.notes: Purple skin and white, dry, chestnut-sweet flesh; Japanese type that stores well and resists pests.

varieties.name: Toma Verde
varieties.notes: Early, large flat-round green fruit; the standard salsa verde tomatillo and reliable in short seasons.

varieties.name: Amarylla
varieties.notes: Small yellow fruits that are sweeter than green types; early and very productive.

varieties.name: Purple de Milpa
varieties.notes: Small purple-blushed fruit with sharper, sweeter flavor; keeps well in the husk for weeks.

varieties.name: Green Malabar
varieties.notes: Basella alba: green stems and glossy leaves; a vigorous climber that keeps cropping through summer heat.

varieties.name: Red Malabar
varieties.notes: Basella rubra: red-purple stems and veins, ornamental on a trellis; same heat-proof summer greens.

varieties.name: Red Leaf
varieties.notes: Green leaves blushed burgundy (sold as red callaloo); cut young for baby greens or let regrow all summer.
